newsitem.title: FRANCE: France's CCBP forecasts market impact of election.
newsitem.headline: France's CCBP forecasts market impact of election.

text.p: French bank Caisse Centrale des Banques Populaires (CCBP) gave the following views in a statement on what it sees as the likely impact on financial markets of three possible outcomes of the March 25/June 1 election -- a Socialist victory, a renewed majority for the centre-right, or no clear majority for either side.
Markets would react in two stages.
"In the period between the announcement of the results and the forming of a government, there could be significant swings."

The bond market, held 90 percent by residents, who generally have a medium-to-long term outlook, is unlikely to react too much, but the stock market, of which non-residents hold 40 percent of portfolio investments and 65 percent of trading positions, "could show a severe correction," it said.
Franc selling "could gather momentum, bringing a real wave of speculation against the French currency".

However, in a second stage, "the market view should become calmer -- assuming the statements of the new prime minister confirm plans to launch the euro on time, with France in a leading role alongside Germany."
CENTRE-RIGHT RPR/UDF COALITION WINS CLEAR NEW MAJORITY

"In the event of a renewal of the current majority in parliament, things would not be significantly different from the previous scenario except on one point, the stock market slide and currency speculation in the first few days would be avoided," it said.

The Paris bourse "could even see a new rise, while on foreign exchange markets the franc could rise steadily to its central rate in the European Exchange Rate Mechanism" (of 3.35 per mark) given the centre-right's determination to launch the euro on time, the continuation of privatisations and implementation of tax cuts for businesses.
NO SIDE EMERGES WITH A CLEAR MAJORITY
"The only real danger which could come from the election would be if it did not produce a clear majority," it said.
This would fuel uncertainty, brake foreign investment and encourage speculation against the franc, with interest focusing on the chances of an interest rate rise.
No clear policies on Europe or the economy could be announced.
The situation would "damage consumer confidence, already at historically low levels, and at the same time, seriously reduce the chances of growth in 1997 of around two percent."
